[Betty Cuningham Gallery welcomes Tibor de Nagy Gallery to Rivington Street]

I am pleased to announce that Tibor de Nagy Gallery, under the leadership of Andrew Arnot, will be joining us on the Lower East Side to share our two spaces here on Rivington Street. The two Galleries will maintain their individual programs and operate under the names of Betty Cuningham Gallery and Tibor de Nagy Gallery.  Each Gallery will continue to have a full season of exhibitions, alternating between the two spaces.

results.title: Contact - Betty Cuningham Gallery
highlights:
[Contact - Betty Cuningham Gallery > A new transition...]

"After two wonderful years at 41 Union Square West #923, I will be taking the next step towards retirement by transitioning the gallery to fully remote operations beginning May 1, 2026.

We will continue to handle sales and inquires as usual; however, my focus will shift to assisting the artists that I have represented for many years with exhibition planning and, gradually, finding new representation. Feel free to contact us directly via email at info@bettycuninghamgallery.com as always. I look forward the flexibility and new opportunities this structure brings – for myself and the artists." - B.C.

Betty Cuningham Gallery will be closing its doors after 20 years.  Our final exhibition - *The Last Picture Show* - will open on Saturday, February 10, from 4 – 6 PM.  It will feature works by several of the gallery’s artists, past and present. The exhibition will remain open to the public through Saturday, April 27, 2024. Detailed announcement to follow. The gallery at 15 Rivington Street will remain open by appointment through May 2024.

As of June 1, 2024 the gallery will transition to a primarily online presence through our website  In this new capacity, we will serve as a resource for our collectors, museums, and curators as we facilitate primary and secondary market sales, acquisitions, publications, research requests and other ongoing projects.

results.title: NYC Selected Gallery Guide, November 2026 – Two Coats of Paint
highlights:
[NYC Selected Gallery Guide, November 2026]

November settles in with a full roster and I’m up for it. In Tribeca, Klaus von Nichtssagend presents Tamara Gonzales, Bortolami has Rebecca Morris, who is looking kind of rosy in the preview image. Is she finally embracing a more traditional form of beauty? We’ll see. At CANADA, Xylor Jane is back with “Paintings for People.” Down on the Lower East Side, Shrine is showing Loren Erdrich while Post Times has a Fergus Feehily show, which seems like a perfect match. In Chelsea, Petzel presents Tschabalala Self, and Nicola Vassell Gallery has LIC pal Pam Glick, who says she never could have made this body of work if she hadn’t moved back to NYC. Julie Curtiss is having her first show at (gasp) Gagosian, and Eric Fischl is back with another solo at Skarstedt. Jason Stopa continues his exploration of brightly-colored architectural forms at Morgan Lehman, and Sherrie Levine is at Galerie Buchholz. If you find yourself in DUMBO, please stop by Springs Projects, 20 Jay Street, Suite 311B, to see “On Certain Grounds,” my show with Cate Holt. The opening is Thursday, November 5, 6-8 pm. I’d love to see you. – *Sharon Butler*

results.title: New York Art Week 2026: Gallery Shows and Prices
highlights:
[As Art Week NYC Kicks Off, Galleries Have Millions of Dollars of Art to Sell—And No Shortage of Naras > Daniel Cassady]

It’s an awkward situation for dealers, who have spent months preparing exhibitions that open around the same time collectors flock into town for the evening sales. **Art Week NYC**, a citywide festival organized by *ARTnews*, *Art in America*, and *Artforum* and running today through Saturday, adds another reason to make the rounds. The galleries have certainly given collectors plenty to look at.

…

Other galleries are taking a less overtly commercial approach. Almine Rech is presenting James Turrell, Greene Naftali has Lubaina Himid, and White Cube is opening a major installation by Doris Salcedo. At 125 Newbury, Mark Rothko and Adolph Gottlieb are paired in an exhibition examining their Surrealist years.

Perhaps the clearest example is Lévy Gorvy Dayan’s exhibition of Francis Bacon and Willem de Kooning. The show is not selling anything. Instead, it brings together works by two postwar giants, demonstrating the sort of scholarship and access that can attract collectors even when there are no prices to negotiate.
